姜泳男.note: Protagonist of Potassium Cyanide: a Korean surgeon, Kyoto-trained, pressed into the Japanese army after the fall of Wuhan and turned Nationalist agent. A fictional character; his Korean name would be read Kang Yong-nam, but the Chinese text and this translation give the Mandarin reading throughout.

唐雅.note: A Chinese-literature student turned Chongqing bailiff and executioner; the woman Jiang is ordered to kill. Fictional; her given name Ya means “refined, elegant.”

杨群.note: Chief of the security bureau in the Police Administration Department, Chongqing; a smooth, controlling policeman of thirty years and Tang Ya's former keeper. Fictional; pinyin.

郭炳炎.note: A captured Nationalist colonel whom Jiang helps escape, later revealed as a powerful figure in the Zhongtong; Jiang's controller. Fictional; pinyin.

唐太太.note: Tang Ya's frail mother, who dies in the Jiaochangkou tunnel disaster. Fictional.

唐先生.note: Tang Ya's father, an engineer at the Hanyang Arsenal, drowned when his boat was sunk on the westward evacuation. Fictional.

姜泳洙.note: Jiang Yongnan's elder brother, a follower of the Korean independence leader Kim Ku. Fictional; pinyin.

岩井.note: Dr. Iwai, the Japanese surgeon whose Hankou clinic Jiang tended; deported when China took back the Japanese concession. Fictional; the surname is read in Japanese as Iwai.

老金.note: The veteran bailiff who oversees the Chongqing executions and watches over Tang Ya. Fictional; “Old” renders the familiar prefix lao.

严副官.note: Guo Bingyan's aide-de-camp. Fictional; fuguan is a military adjutant.

安德森.note: An American diplomatic attaché, killed by Jiang in the back alley of the White Night bar. Fictional; the source's transliteration.

小坂次郎.note: A Japanese newspaper correspondent whose feature on Jiang makes him a propaganda figure. Fictional; the name read in Japanese.

祁先生.note: The Nationalist intelligence handler who first recruits Jiang, passing him the cyanide-filled coin. Fictional; pinyin.

金九.note: Kim Ku (1876–1949), leader of the Korean independence movement and of the Provisional Government in exile; wounded in the 1938 Changsha shooting. Historical; attested Korean romanization.

中原司令部.note: The novella's name for the Japanese army command in the Wuhan region, where Jiang serves as a military doctor. Zhongyuan means “the Central Plains”; not a standard historical designation.

中央警校.note: The Central Police Academy (Nanjing, 1936), the Nationalists' police-officer school; Dai Li ran it as superintendent and used it to recruit for the Juntong.

警政司.note: The police-administration bureau of the Ministry of the Interior, where Yang Qun heads the security bureau.

保安处.note: The security office within the Police Administration Department; Yang Qun's posting.

汉阳兵器厂.note: China's oldest modern ordnance works, at Hanyang; dismantled and shipped west ahead of the Japanese advance.

兵工署.note: The National Government's ordnance directorate, which oversaw the arsenals and paid the arsenal workers' death benefits.

红十字会.note: The Red Cross; Jiang served with its Hankou branch before his arrest.

东京日日新闻.note: A major Japanese daily (1872–1943), forerunner of the Mainichi Shimbun; the paper that ran the propaganda feature on Jiang.

中央党部.note: The central headquarters of the Nationalist Party; Jiang carries its credentials, cover for his intelligence work.

派遣军.note: The Japan China Expeditionary Army, the umbrella command for Japanese forces in China, into which Jiang is conscripted as a colonial subject.

隆盛参茸行.note: A Shapingba shop dealing in ginseng and deer-antler, a front for a Japanese intelligence station. Fictional.

汉口.note: One of the three towns of Wuhan, on the north bank of the Yangtze; site of Jiang's clinic and of the former Japanese concession.

武昌.note: One of the three towns of Wuhan, on the south bank; site of the university requisitioned as a Japanese hospital.

武昌大学.note: The source's name for the university at Mount Luojia, whose canteen becomes the Japanese wounded-soldiers' hospital; the campus is National Wuhan University's.

珞珈山.note: The wooded hill in Wuchang on which National Wuhan University stands.

四杂街.note: The Hankou street where the Iwai clinic and the little church stood. The name's first character means “four”; it is not a count.

东湖.note: The large lake east of Wuchang, across which Jiang rows the escaping Guo Bingyan.

广州.note: The southern port city (Canton) where Jiang's brother is said to have gone.

长沙.note: Capital of Hunan; site of the 1938 shooting of Kim Ku and a way-station of the Korean Provisional Government.

沙坪坝.note: A district of wartime Chongqing, thick with schools, offices, and government hostels.

朝天门码头.note: Chongqing's principal wharf, at the tip of the peninsula where the Jialing meets the Yangtze.

川东师范.note: A teachers' college in Chongqing; in the story, the Zhongtong's public front.

莲花池.note: A Chongqing street corner with a Korean noodle shop, Jiang's planned rendezvous.

莲花湖.note: A lake near the Longsheng shop, where Jiang's body is to be “found.”

安溪.note: A county in Fujian, Yang Qun's birthplace and the home of Tieguanyin tea.

涪陵.note: A district on the Yangtze upstream of Chongqing, source of the local rice liquor in the bar's cocktail.

中华路.note: A street in central Chongqing; the White Night bar stands at its junction with Linjiangmen.

临江门.note: A gate and district on the Jialing side of old Chongqing.

White night酒吧.note: A Chongqing bar, once a foreign correspondents' club. Fictional; the source keeps the English name.

法警.note: A court officer of the judicial police; here the corps also carries out the death sentences it guards.

氰化钾.note: The fast-acting poison that gives the novella its title; carried by agents as a means of suicide on capture.

铁观音.note: A prized oolong tea from Anxi in Fujian; “Iron Goddess of Mercy.”

驼峰.note: The Allied airlift route over the eastern Himalayas from India to Nationalist China after the Burma Road was cut.

禁娱令.note: The wartime government's prohibition of dance halls and public amusements in the capital.

土地庙.note: A small shrine to the local earth-god (Tudi), the humblest deity of Chinese folk religion; here a hiding place for a wireless set.

ch31.note: “Devils” (guizi) was the standard wartime Chinese epithet for the Japanese; “running dog” (zougou, here “lackey”) for one who served them. Unable to place a Korean prisoner, the interrogator reaches for both at once. Texture.

The Battle of Wuhan (June–October 1938) was the largest engagement of the war's early years; Japanese forces took the city on 27 October 1938, and the Nationalist government, already withdrawn upriver, made Chongqing its wartime capital in earnest. Wuhan is the union of three towns on the Yangtze — Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang. Historical (corroborated).

ch31.anchor: taking back the Japanese concession in Hankou
ch31.note: Hankou held a cluster of foreign concessions; the Japanese one dated from 1898. After full-scale war broke out in 1937 its Japanese residents withdrew, and on 13 August 1938 the Nationalist government took the concession over as the Hankou No. 4 Special Zone — the event the story places “a year after the Battle of Shanghai.” Japan reclaimed it on occupying the city that October and in 1943 nominally ceded it to the Wang Jingwei regime. Historical (corroborated).

Kyoto Imperial University (founded 1897) was one of imperial Japan's two oldest and most prestigious universities, its medical faculty among the finest in the empire. That a colonial Korean holds such a degree is the very thing the Japanese officer later trades on. Historical.

Kim Ku (1876–1949), leader of the Korean independence movement and a head of the Provisional Government in exile. On 7 May 1938, at a gathering of Korean parties in the Nammok Hall in Changsha, a disaffected Korean, Yi Un-han, opened fire; one delegate was killed and Kim Ku gravely wounded, though he survived. This is the “shooting in Changsha.” Historical (corroborated).

ch31.anchor: the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea
ch31.note: The Korean Provisional Government, formed in Shanghai in 1919 after the March First independence movement, was the exile government of the Korean cause; through the war it moved with the Chinese Nationalists across the country — Changsha, then Chongqing — which is why its adherents turn up here in wartime China. Historical (corroborated).

The priest's phrase renders the idiom luoye guigen, “fallen leaves return to their roots” — the wish to die and be buried in one's native soil. In his mouth it is doubled: a Korean exile's longing for a homeland under Japanese rule, and the reason he serves the independence cause behind his cassock. Idiom (texture).

The “Expeditionary Army” (pai-qian jun) is the Japan China Expeditionary Army, the command for Japanese forces in China. As a colonial subject of the empire, Jiang is liable to its call-up, and refusal, as the officer implies, carried grave penalties. Historical.

ch31.anchor: So her name was Tang Ya
ch31.note: Her given name, Ya (雅), means “refined, elegant, cultivated” — the word for a lettered young woman, apt for the Chinese-literature student she was. The novella will set that name against what the war makes of her, a bar-haunting executioner; the irony is there for a Chinese reader at the first sight of the character. Texture (telling name).

ch32.note: A documented detail: after taking Wuhan the Japanese army turned the National Wuhan University campus at Mount Luojia (the story's “Wuchang University”) into a hospital for its wounded, and in the spring of 1939 planted the first cherry trees there to ease the men's homesickness. Those trees are the origin of the university's now-famous cherry blossoms. Historical (corroborated).

“Shina” (Chinese Zhina) was the name Japan used for China in this period. Neutral in origin, it became in imperial and wartime usage a term of contempt, rejected by the Chinese as a slur. The propaganda headline's “in Shina” is the occupier's word for the country it is invading. Historical (corroborated).

The “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere” was Japan's slogan for the bloc of Asian territories it claimed to be freeing from Western rule and uniting under its own leadership — in practice the ideological cover for conquest. A Korean doctor tending Chinese poor made ideal propaganda for it. Historical (corroborated).

The Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun (1872–1943) was one of Japan's major dailies, tied to the Osaka Mainichi and a forerunner of today's Mainichi Shimbun; in the war years it carried the army's line. Historical (corroborated).

ch32.anchor: a great man can bend and can stretch
ch32.note: The proverb da zhangfu neng qu neng shen, “a great man can bend and can stretch” — that is, endure humiliation now to prevail later, a maxim of strategic patience. The priest uses it to keep Jiang inside the enemy's uniform. Idiom (texture).

From the set phrase tiao jin Huang He ye xi bu qing, “even leaping into the Yellow River you couldn't wash yourself clean” — said of a disgrace or suspicion no protest can rinse away (the Yellow River runs thick with silt). Jiang means his complicity is now indelible. Idiom (texture).
The meiyu, or “plum rains” — the long, humid rainy season of the middle and lower Yangtze in early summer, named for its coincidence with the ripening of the plums. Climate / custom.

Potassium cyanide, a fast-acting poison, was the agent's standard means of suicide on capture; here it is sealed in wax inside a hollowed silver dollar, the piece of tradecraft the novella takes for its title. Guo will later call it “the last gift a killer keeps for himself.” Note that it is passed as a means of self-destruction, not of murder — the axis on which the plot turns. Historical / motif.

ch33.note: The Pacific War opened with Japan's attacks on Pearl Harbor and Southeast Asia in December 1941, bringing the United States into the conflict; wartime Chongqing filled with American servicemen and correspondents, the clientele the bar reflects. Historical (corroborated).

“The Hump” was the airlift route Allied transports flew over the eastern Himalayas from India to supply Nationalist China after the Burma Road was cut in 1942 — punishing, high-altitude flying with heavy losses. The young captain has just crossed it. Historical (corroborated).

The Central Police Academy (Nanjing, 1936) trained the Nationalists' police officers. Chiang Kai-shek was its titular head, but Dai Li — chief of the Juntong, the military secret service — ran it as superintendent and used it, as the passage says, to recruit young cadets into the Juntong and plant them through the government. So a graduate of the academy might well be a Juntong agent in disguise, which is why Guo distrusts Tang Ya. Historical (corroborated).

ch33.anchor: mend the fold after the sheep is lost
ch33.note: The chengyu wang yang bu lao, “to mend the fold after the sheep are lost” — to repair a fault after harm is done, before worse follows; usually reassuring, “better late than never.” Guo turns it cold, on the loose end Tang Ya represents. Idiom (texture).

ch33.anchor: What youth is not moved by love
ch33.note: Guo quotes, in colloquial form, a couplet Chinese readers know from Guo Moruo's celebrated translation of Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther: roughly, “What young man is not stirred to love? What maiden does not yearn in spring?” A worldly, faintly mocking gloss on the bond he suspects between Jiang and Tang Ya. Allusion (corroborated).

ch33.anchor: the twenty-seventh year of the Republic
ch33.note: Dates in Republican China were counted from the founding of the Republic in 1912, so “the twenty-seventh year of the Republic” is 1938, the year Wuhan fell. Historical (corroborated).

ch34.anchor: the air-raid tunnel disaster at Jiaochangkou
ch34.note: The Jiaochangkou tunnel disaster (5 June 1941): during a prolonged Japanese night raid on Chongqing, huge crowds packed into a public shelter near Jiaochangkou whose entrances were kept sealed, and mass suffocation and trampling followed — the deadliest single incident of the Chongqing bombing. The toll is disputed: Nationalist figures put it near a thousand, later accounts at 2,500 or more, and popular memory (like the source's “tens of thousands”) far higher. The exact number was never fixed. Historical (corroborated; toll contested).

The Hanyang Arsenal, founded in the 1890s by the reformer Zhang Zhidong, was China's oldest modern ordnance works and the maker of the “Hanyang-made” rifle carried through decades of war; like much of China's industry it was dismantled and shipped west, up the Yangtze, ahead of the Japanese advance. Historical (corroborated).

In the wartime capital the Nationalist government issued bans on dance halls and public amusements (the jin yu ling, “ban on entertainment”) as unbecoming a nation at war — which is how the raids that shut the halls brought Tang Ya to Yang Qun's notice. Historical.

ch34.anchor: watching the stump for a hare
ch34.note: The chengyu shou zhu dai tu, “to watch the tree stump waiting for a hare” — from the fable of a farmer who, having once seen a hare run into a stump and die, gave up his plow to wait by it for another. It means to sit idle for a windfall; Tang Ya turns it on the men lying in wait for Jiang. Idiom (texture).

ch34.anchor: a worn shoe on another man's foot
ch34.note: “A worn shoe” (po xie) is Chinese slang for a woman of loose reputation. Old Jin's silent pity is exactly this: he sees Tang Ya throwing herself away, and the phrase carries the judgment even as he grieves it. Slang (texture).

ch35.note: The story has the Zhongtong — the Nationalist Party's civil secret service — keep its known office, a mere signboard, at the East Sichuan Normal School, while its real work is done in an unmarked house by the wharf. Hiding the working headquarters behind a public front was standard tradecraft for both Nationalist services; the specific placement here is the novella's, not a matter of record. Institutional (plausible).
Chaotianmen, at the tip of the peninsula where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze, is Chongqing's oldest and largest wharf and the water gateway to the mountain city. Geographic (corroborated).

Tieguanyin (“Iron Goddess of Mercy”) is a prized oolong from Anxi county in Fujian; “spring water, autumn fragrance” evokes its seasonal picking. By pouring Yang Qun the tea of his own birthplace, Guo shows without a word how thoroughly he has read the man's file. Material culture (corroborated).

ch35.anchor: a fish that slipped the net
ch35.note: The chengyu lou wang zhi yu, “a fish that slipped through the net” — one who escapes a dragnet. Guo means Jiang's corpse, which Yang Qun is to “discover” with a scalpel planted on it, so the killing of the American passes as the work of a Japanese spy run to ground. Idiom (texture).

ch35.anchor: lick blood from the knife's edge
ch35.note: Dao tou tian xue, “to lick blood from the edge of the knife” — to live by killing, a hair from death; the trade of the assassin. Guo invokes the danger of their calling to justify letting Jiang keep the woman. Idiom (texture).

ch35.anchor: a needle at the bottom of the sea
ch35.note: From the proverb nuren xin, hai di zhen — “a woman's heart is a needle at the bottom of the sea,” impossible to fathom or to retrieve. Guo's parting word undercuts his own generosity: he has handed Jiang the woman, but not her heart. Proverb (texture).

“Lukewarm water” (wen-tun shui) is said of a tepid, spineless person who will neither boil nor freeze. It is Tang Ya's contemptuous name for Yang Qun's unshakable, fatherly patience — the very evenness she wants to crack. Idiom (texture).
